newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt radio channel attracts mainland interest.
newsitem.headline: HK govt radio channel attracts mainland interest.

text.p: A tiny new Hong Kong government-sponsored radio channel which broadcasts entirely in China's Mandarin tongue could suddenly find itself the reluctant leader of a radio revolution on the mainland.

"We've had proposals of cooperation from dozens of mainland Chinese radio stations located everywhere between Guangdong and Heilongjiang (in north China)," channel chief Cheung Kwai Yeung told Reuters.
Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK) launched a channel on AM 621 that broadcasts entirely in the sculpted tones of "Putonghua", or plain speech, the official language of mainland China.
This immediately made vibrant, Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong accessible to mainland Chinese radio broadcasters thirsting to expand their repertoires, Cheung said.
"When these Chinese radio stations heard there was a Putonghua channel in Hong Kong, they wanted to establish connections and borrow new elements, new programme ideas, new stimuli," Cheung said.
China's radio industry has traditionally pioneered media reform and is far ahead of the lumbering print and television media reputed to be government mouthpieces, Cheung said.
"After July 1 we could well be cooperating with a radio station in Guangdong province," said Cheung, adding that negotiations were currently under way.
Radio stations all over China, except in Tibet and the Moslem-majority province of Xinjiang, are required by law to broadcast in Putonghua, not in local dialects, Cheung said.
"This makes cooperation with a Cantonese radio station very difficult for a mainland station," Cheung said.
AM 621 was initially launched to help new immigrants arriving in Hong Kong from China find housing, understand the legal system and get medical help.
Much to the channel's surprise, phone-in programmes revealed a local stronghold of older, established immigrants who still yearned for a bit of home and a familiar language.
Now, far from worrying about Chinese government intervention, Hong Kong could be spearheading a few changes of its own over the border.
